***The Dullah Diaries***

## Chapter 1: The Longest Ride Ever

***Monday, November 3rd***

***Just got off the world's most ancient taxi after what felt like a million hours. It was only supposed to be seven, but trust me, my butt says it was way longer.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah in the back of a cramped taxi, squished between a chicken cage and a woman holding the cage, looking miserable.]

***Finally, we stop in front of this shop that's supposed to be my "welcome to your new life" spot or something. The sign says "Vonnie's," but it looks like it survived a couple of wars itself.***

[Illustration suggestion: A ramshackle shop with a skewed sign reading "Vonnie's," and Abdullah standing outside with his giant suitcase, looking confused.]

***Did I mention I've been orphaned? Yeah. Thanks to some stupid war back home in Congo. Mom and Dad were heroes, fighting for the good guys, and then—bam!—they're gone. And here I am, dumped in South Africa with some uncle I've never even heard of.***

***Been sitting on this rock for ages, watching people go in and out of the shop. I started throwing pebbles at my big toe because, you know, boredom. Then, out of nowhere, the sun decides to bail on me. I look up, and there's this super tall shadow looming over me.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah sitting on a rock, tossing pebbles at his toe, with a long shadow suddenly appearing over him.]

***The shadows all like, "You, Lizzie’s boy? You Dullah?" His voice sounds like he's been gargling gravel.***

***It takes me a second to realize he's talking about my mom, Elizabeth. So I tell him I'm Abdullah, but he's already telling me to hurry up because the goats won't wait. Like I care about goats right now.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah, squinting up at a tall, shadowy figure, with a thought bubble that says, "Who's Lizzie?"]

***Turns out the shadow guy is actually pretty short. It's Uncle Jan, who seems like he's been wrestling with life since he was born. And those eyes—man, if looks could kill, I'd be pushing up daisies right next to that sign.***

***He tells me I'm Dullah now, he doesn’t have time for long names, which I guess is his way of saying "Welcome to the family." Then he points to this donkey cart that's supposed to take us home. It's like something out of an old movie where everything goes wrong.***

[Illustration suggestion: A short, tough-looking Uncle Jan with steely eyes, standing next to a donkey cart, with Abdullah looking down at him, taken aback.]

***So, here I am, sitting on a cart that's bumping along like it's got a grudge against me, heading to a place I've never seen before. And all I can think is: what kind of weird adventure have I gotten myself into?***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah on a rickety cart, holding onto his suitcase for dear life as the donkeys pull him along a dusty road.]
---

## Chapter 2: The New Crew and the Classroom Encounter

***Monday, January 13th***

***The holidays are over, and I've definitely earned my stripes working on Uncle Jan's goat farm. I mean, who knew goats had so much... personality? And now, school's about to start. Greeaaat….***
[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah with a pitchfork, surrounded by goats, one of which is chewing on his shirt.]
***So there I am, setting off for Low Water Primary. It's a 7 km trek, and I'm not even kidding. By the time I reach the school gates, it feels like I've joined this parade of kids. They're all sizes and shapes, but next to me? They look like they're still in preschool.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah towering over a line of much smaller kids, looking bewildered.]

***Then, out of the blue, there's this girl, Berenice. She's jogging up like it's no big deal, and you can tell she's one of those sporty types. She gives me this look, head to toe, with a smile that says, "You're not from around here, are you?" Feels like I'm on display at some exotic animal exhibit.***

[Illustration suggestion: Berenice sizing up Abdullah with a curious smile as he awkwardly tries to ignore the attention.]

***At school, things don't get any better. I'm like the main attraction at a circus. Girls are all giggles and whispers, and the boys? They've got this "who's the new guy?" look plastered all over their faces.***

***Uncle Jan, in his infinite wisdom, told me first things first: meet the principal. That guys a dead ringer for Mr. Miyagi from "The Karate Kid." I half-expected him to start giving me wax-on, wax-off lessons right there.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah standing nervously in front of the principal's desk, while the principal, who looks like Mr. Miyagi, eyes him curiously.]

***Mr. Miyagi, I mean, the principal, marches me over to meet my Grade 6 teacher, Mr. Jones. Imagine a bear in a sweater, and you've got the right picture. He growls something about tucking in my shirt and not slouching, and I'm just nodding like one of those bobblehead dolls.***

***In the classroom, there's this kid in the back corner, all alone, scribbling away like he's trying to win some kind of homework marathon. Who even does that before the bell rings? He's got these bright, shiny shoes, looking like theyve never stepped in a puddle, let alone a goat pen…and here I’m standing with both big toes covered in dust!***

[Illustration suggestion: A studious kid with a focused expression, sitting at a desk piled with books, while others are playing around him.]

***And this kids not just a shiny-shoed wonder; everything about him screams brand new. It's like he's the human version of a fresh notebook at the start of the term.***
***Just when I thought I could slip out and avoid more of this first-day zoo, the shiny kid stands up. He's got so much Vaseline on his hair and face, I'm worried he might slip right out of his chair. He looks like a walking, talking Back to School advert.***

[Illustration suggestion: A boy with slick, shiny hair and a face so glossy it reflects light, standing confidently with a hand outstretched.]

***He walks over, hand out like he's running for class president or something, and hits me with, "Hi, I'm Brian, and yes, my dad*** **is *as dangerous as he looks."***

***I'm standing there, trying to figure out if that's a warning or a weird flex, but I shake his hand anyway. It's like shaking hands with a tub of margarine.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah looking confused as he shakes a greasy-handed Brians hand, with a thought bubble that reads, "Should I be worried about his dad?"]

***Brian starts rattling on about how his dads the deputy disciplinarian or something,and how he can fix any bad choice with his special sticks, whatever that means.***
***I'm just nodding, still trying to figure out if I'm supposed to be impressed or scared.***
***The bell rings, and the classroom suddenly fills up like someone turned on the kid-tap. They're all taking seats, sneaking peeks at me and Brian, probably trying to suss out the new dynamics.***

[Illustration suggestion: Kids flooding into the classroom, with various expressions of curiosity and amusement directed at Abdullah and Brian.]

***Mr. Jones claps his hands for attention, and that's my cue to find a seat. The only one left is right next to Brian, go figure. So now I'm the new kid with the shiny sidekick. This is going to be an interesting year.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah sitting awkwardly next to a grinning Brian, both surrounded by a sea of curious faces.]

***As Mr. Jones starts talking about the importance of good choices, hard work and dedication, I can't help but let my mind wander. I'm thinking about how I ended up here, in this strange new world that's so different from my old life. I'm wondering if I'll ever fit in, if I'll ever understand the rules of this place, or if I'll always be the odd one out.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah daydreaming at his desk; a thought bubble shows a montage of his old home, the journey to his uncles, and the faces of his new classmates.]

***But then I catch Berenices eye from across the room, and she gives me a thumbs-up. It's a small gesture, but it feels like a lifeline. Maybe, just maybe, I won't have to navigate this all on my own.***

[Illustration suggestion: Berenice giving Abdullah a supportive thumbs-up from across the room, with Abdullah looking surprised but grateful.]

***Lunchtime rolls around, and I find myself sitting with Brian and a few other kids who don't seem to mind the newness oozing off of me. They're a ragtag bunch: there's a quiet girl who's always reading, a guy who claims he can eat ten sandwiches in one go, and a pair of twins who finish each others sentences.***

[Illustration suggestion: A diverse group of kids sitting at a lunch table, with Abdullah in the middle looking a bit overwhelmed by his chatty new friends.]

***We're the misfits, the leftovers, the ones who don't quite fit into the neat little boxes of school social life. But as we share stories and laugh at Brians dad jokes, I start to feel like maybe I've found my gang. They're weird and wonderful, and they don't care that I'm the tall African kid with an accent.***

[Illustration suggestion: The group laughing together, with Abdullah starting to smile genuinely for the first time.]

***By the end of the day, my farm brain is exhausted but hopeful. This place is nothing like home, and I miss my parents more than ever. But I've got a feeling that these people, this odd little community, might just become something like a family to me.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah walking home from school, a small smile on his face, the sun setting behind him, casting a long shadow ahead.]

## Chapter 3: Finding My Feet

***Tuesday, January 14th***
***Day two at Low Water Primary, and I already have a routine: dodge the chickens, jump the fence, and start the long walk to school. It's not so bad when you've got company, even if that company is a bunch of kids half your size with twice your energy.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah leaping over a fence, with chickens scattering and kids cheering him on in the background.]

***Today, Berenice caught up with me again. She's got this way of smiling like she's in on a joke nobody else knows about. She asked me about Congo, and I told her a bit—how it's nothing like here, how I miss the music and the food. She just listened, nodding like she understood, even though I could tell this was all a world away for her.***

[Illustration suggestion: Berenice jogging next to Abdullah, who's talking and gesturing with his hands, a nostalgic look on his face.]

***In class, Mr. Jones handed out a math test like a morning greeting. I barely had time to write my name before the numbers started swimming in front of my eyes. Brian, though, he was scribbling away like it was Christmas and the test was his present.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah staring blankly at a test paper, while Brian next to him writes with gusto, a determined glint in his eye.]

***At lunch, I sat with my new gang again. The sandwich guy, who'se name is Mervin, actually tried to eat those ten sandwiches (most of them from Brian’s lunch). He got to seven before he turned a shade of green I'd only seen on sick goats. The reading girl, Gwen, didnt even look up from her book, just passed him a napkin like shed seen it all before.***

[Illustration suggestion: Tom with a pile of sandwich crusts, looking queasy, while Sarah nonchalantly reads her book and offers a napkin without looking.]

***The twins, Gerald and Geraldine (yes, really), kept everyone entertained with their magic tricks. They're not half bad, unless you count Geraldines tendency to reveal the secret if you laugh at her jokes. I think they might be my favorite people here.***

[Illustration suggestion: Gerald pulling a coin from behind Geraldines ear, while she's about to spill the beans with a wide grin, and Abdullah chuckles.]

***After school, Berenice invited me to join their impromptu soccer game. I havent played in forever, but it was like riding a bike—you don't forget how to dodge and weave, even if the goats are your usual opponents.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah in the middle of a makeshift soccer game, skillfully maneuvering the ball away from a lunging defender.]
***Turns out, I'm not half bad, and by the end of the game, even the kids whod been giving me side-eyes in the morning were slapping my back and saying, "Not bad for a newbie." It felt good, like I'd earned a little piece of respect on this strange new turf.***

[Illustration suggestion: Kids from the soccer game surrounding Abdullah, some giving thumbs up, others clapping him on the back.]

***As the sun dipped low and the shadows stretched out, I walked back to Uncle Jan's farm, the chatter and laughter of my new friends echoing in my mind. For the first time since I got here, I didnt feel quite so alone.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah walking home with a soccer ball under his arm, a content smile on his face, as the sun sets behind the familiar silhouette of the farm.]

***Today was a good day. And maybe, just maybe, I'll have more of them here. Maybe I can carve out a slice of home in this new place, with these new people. It's not Congo, but it's starting to feel a little bit like mine.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah looking back at the school in the distance, a hopeful gaze in his eyes, as the last light of day glows on the horizon.]

***As I walked, the laughter of my new friends still warming my heart, I realized something important. This place, with it's odd customs and unfamiliar faces, was slowly becoming a part of me. It wasnt just the soccer game or the jokes at lunch. It was the small moments, the nods of understanding, and the shared struggles in class that were weaving into the fabric of my daily life.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah with a thoughtful expression, small moments from his day like a shared joke, a nod from Berenice, and a high-five from Brian, all floating around his head like memories.]

***When I finally saw Uncle Jan's farm on the horizon, the goats bleating their welcome, it didnt feel so foreign anymore. This farm, these animals, the dusty path I walked every day—they were becoming my new routine, my new normal.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah approaching the farm, with goats in the foreground greeting him; the farm is bathed in the warm, golden light of the setting sun.]

***As I closed the gate behind me and the last light of the day faded, I felt a quiet sense of achievement. Today, I wasnt just the new kid from a far-off place. I was Abdullah, the soccer player, the friend, the part of something. And that thought alone made me eager to see what tomorrow would bring.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah closing the farm gate, looking back at the path behind him, a determined and hopeful look on his face as the stars begin to twinkle in the twilight sky.]

***This place might never replace the home I'd lost, but it was offering me something precious—a chance to grow roots in new soil, to become part of a community, and to build a life that honored the memory of my parents. I went to bed that night with a smile, thinking, "Bring it on, Low Water Primary. I'm ready for you now."***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah lying in bed, a content smile on his face, the room dimly lit by a small bedside lamp, with a diary open next to him on the nightstand.]

***And with that thought, I drifted off to sleep, the sounds of the farm lulling me into dreams of tomorrows adventures.***

---

## Chapter 4: The Dusty Track and Rivalry Begins

***Friday, February 7th***

***You can feel the buzz in the air today. It's Athletics Day at Low Water Primary, and every kids got that look of pure excitement. Well, almost every kid. Me? I can't see what's so special about a bunch of white lines on sandy dirt. Mr. Jones and the Grade 6 class spent all of Friday getting the track ready, and I still don't get it. It's just dust with boundaries.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah looking unimpressed at the track while other kids around him are buzzing with excitement.]

***I've always been decent at sports, so I'm cautiously optimistic about my chances today. But there's this guy, Richard—Brians best bud—tall, lean, and a stamina machine. He's been the school's track hero since forever, and everyone expects him to sweep the long distance again.***

***The day kicks off early, and surprise, surprise—Richards taking gold in the 1500m and 800m. But as the distances get shorter, I start closing the gap. By the time the 400m comes around, I'm right on his heels, and the crowds starting to take notice.***

[Illustration suggestion: Richard crossing the finish line with Abdullah just a step behind, both panting and sweaty.]

***Sprints are my jam. I can feel the power in my legs, the kind of muscle you get from chasing goats, not from running in circles. So when the 200m starts, and I leave everyone in the dust, Richards smile starts to wobble. The cheers for me are getting louder, and the look on his face tells me he didnt see this coming.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah surging ahead in the 200m sprint, with a crowd of students cheering wildly in the background.]

***When the 100m dash comes around, I'm ready. I explode off the line, and it's like I'm back home, running through the fields, free and unstoppable. I cross the finish line first, and it feels like flying.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah in full sprint, a blur to the onlookers, crossing the finish line with a clear lead.]

***Richards not clapping, though. When I offer my hand in a sportsmanlike shake, he just stares at it like it's a dead fish. I retract my hand, a little sting of disappointment hitting me, but I brush it off. It's just a race, right?***

***Then there's Berenice, Richards girl—or at least, that's what everyone thought. She's over here, jumping up and down, and I swear she's more excited about my win than I am. She throws her arms around me, and I can feel every pair of eyes on the field burning into my back, especially Richards.***

[Illustration suggestion: Berenice hugging Abdullah, who looks surprised and awkward, as Richard glares at them from the background.]

***That's when I feel it—the shift. It's not just about a race anymore. It's not just about who's the fastest. It's something more, something deeper, and I can tell this is only the beginning. Richards face is hard, his eyes cold, and I know that whatever this year was going to be, it just got a lot more complicated.***

[Illustration suggestion: Richards face, twisted in a mix of anger and jealousy, watching Abdullah and Berenice celebrating.]

***As the day winds down and the dust settles on the makeshift track, I realize that I've won more than just a race today. I've won the attention I wasnt sure I wanted, made a rival I didnt mean to make, and somehow, I've stepped into a war that I didnt even know was being fought.***

[Illustration suggestion: Abdullah sitting alone on the bleachers, looking pensive as he watches the deserted track, the setting sun casting long shadows.]

***But one things for sure: I'm not backing down. This is my life now, and I'm going to live it on my terms, running full speed ahead. Bring it on, Richard. I'm just getting started.***

---

---

## Chapter 5: The Choir Catastrophe

*Friday, February 14th*

Choir practice. Just when I thought school couldnt get any weirder, they decided to throw singing into the mix. I shuffled into the music room, which smelled faintly of old books and chalk—a stark contrast to the open air I'm used to. The younger kids buzzed around like excited bees, their voices already warming up. I felt like a giant among them, sticking out like a sore thumb.

"Abdullah, back row with the taller boys!" Mrs. Llucing snapped, pointing her ever-present ruler toward the bench. Her eyes were sharp behind her tiny glasses, and I got the feeling she didnt tolerate nonsense.

I made my way to the back, squeezing between Gerald and Mervin. The bench wobbled under our combined weight. Mrs. Llucing tapped her music stand. "Attention, everyone! From the top!"

We launched into some song about rivers and mountains. I mumbled along, trying to be invisible. But then came a high note that everyone else seemed to hit effortlessly. I took a deep breath and went for it.

My voice cracked so loudly it echoed off the walls. Silence fell. Then, like a dam breaking, the back row erupted into laughter. My cheeks burned hotter than the sun back home.

"Nice one," Gerald snickered, nudging me. Mortified, I shifted my weight, accidentally knocking into him. Everything seemed to go in slow motion as Gerald flailed and toppled off the bench, landing with a thud.

"Hey! Watch it!" Richard snapped, stepping forward to help Gerald up. His eyes met mine, a storm brewing. "You did that on purpose!"

"It was an accident," I protested, my heart pounding.

"Sure didnt look like it," he retorted, squaring up to me. The room had shrunk; all eyes were on us.

"Enough!" Mrs. Llucings voice sliced through the tension. She marched over, ruler in hand, her face a mix of fury and exasperation. "I've had it with you Grade Sixes! Out! Both of you! Go find Mr. Jones immediately!"

I glanced at Richard, who'se glare hadnt softened. Without another word, we shuffled out of the room, the door closing behind us with a decisive click.

The hallway was quiet except for the distant hum of other classes. My stomach twisted. Facing Mr. Jones was the last thing I wanted to do.

"Great job, newbie," Richard muttered, not bothering to look at me.

I clenched my fists but said nothing. Arguing wouldnt help. Besides, a part of me knew this was bigger than a choir mishap. This was about everything—Athletics Day, Berenice, being the new kid who didnt know his place.

We walked in tense silence toward Mr. Jones office, each step heavier than the last. I could feel the weight of the upcoming confrontation pressing down on me.

As we reached the door, I took a deep breath, trying to steady myself. This wasnt how I imagined my day going. But then again, nothing since arriving here had been as I'd imagined.

Richard knocked, and a gruff voice beckoned us inside. Time to face the music—pun intended.

---

## Chapter 6: Latrine Duty Disaster

**Monday, February 17th**

Standing in Mr. Jones’ office, I had never been more aware of how much trouble I was in. My feet felt like they were glued to the floor, and I could feel Richard shifting next to me, arms crossed, still fuming. Mr. Jones sat at his desk, staring us down like we were bugs under a magnifying glass.

"Disrupting choir practice, knocking each other around, and turning the room into a circus," Mr. Jones began, his voice low and controlled, which somehow made it even scarier. "What exactly do you two think you're doing?"

Neither of us answered. There wasn’t much to say that wouldn’t make things worse. My mind raced as I tried to come up with something—anything—that could explain why we’d acted like idiots in choir. But before I could even open my mouth, Mr. Jones cut in.

"I don’t want excuses," he snapped. "I want solutions. Clearly, you two have a problem. And since you can’t solve it on your own, we’ll give you something to work on together."

My stomach dropped. That didn’t sound good.

"Starting today," Mr. Jones continued, "you’ll be helping Mr. Hendricks with latrine duty for the rest of the week. After school. Every day."

Latrine duty. The words hung in the air like the smell of the farm's worst goat pen. I didn’t know what was worse—the idea of cleaning out the school’s pit toilets, or the fact that I had to do it with Richard.

Mr. Jones must’ve seen the horror on my face, because he leaned back in his chair and smiled—a thin, humorless smile. "Maybe some time spent doing real work will help you two figure out how to get along."

Before I could protest, Richard spoke up. "Whatever. Fine."

That was all Mr. Jones needed to hear. "You’re dismissed," he said, waving his hand toward the door. "Meet Mr. Hendricks after school. He’ll show you what to do."

We shuffled out of the office without a word. My stomach was doing backflips, but Richard’s face was set in stone, as if this whole thing didn’t bother him at all. I, on the other hand, couldn’t help but feel like I was walking into some kind of nightmare.

---


**Later that Afternoon**

The bell rang, signaling the end of the school day. Normally, that sound was music to my ears, but today it felt like the tolling of doom. I made my way over to the janitor’s shed behind the school, where I found Richard already waiting, leaning against the door with his arms crossed and a scowl on his face.

Mr. Hendricks, the school janitor, appeared a minute later. He was a short, grizzled man with thick glasses that made his eyes look twice as big as they should be. He gave us both a look that clearly said he wasn’t impressed.

"So, you two are the new recruits, huh?" he said, scratching his scruffy chin. "Well, let’s not waste time. Follow me."

He led us around the back of the school to the pit toilets—six squat, rundown outhouses that made the goat pens at Uncle Jan’s farm look like a five-star hotel. The smell hit me before we even got close, and I had to fight the urge to gag. Richard didn’t flinch, but I noticed him wrinkle his nose.

"Here’s how it works," Mr. Hendricks said, gesturing toward the outhouses with a grim smile. "Each of these toilets has a bucket underneath. You’ll be emptying them into these larger bins." He pointed to two massive metal containers on wheels. "Once the bins are full, you’ll wheel them down to the sewage tank at the bottom of the hill."

I could already see where this was going, and I didn’t like it one bit.

"Any questions?" Mr. Hendricks asked, not that he really cared. "No? Good. Get to work."

He tossed us each a pair of gloves and bandanas to tie over our faces, but it didn’t do much to block out the stench. I pulled the bandana over my nose and got to work, gagging slightly as I opened the first toilet and saw the disgusting sight waiting for me. Richard, to his credit, didn’t complain. He just started working in silence.

It didn’t take long before the first of the big bins was full. Richard and I each grabbed a handle, lifting the heavy bin and struggling to get it onto the wheelbarrows Mr. Hendricks had left for us. The wheels creaked as we pushed the barrows toward the steep hill behind the school.

"We’ve gotta be careful," I muttered, mostly to myself. "If we go too fast—"

"Relax," Richard interrupted. "It’s not that hard. We just have to get this to the bottom. Piece of cake."

I shot him a look but didn’t argue. The hill was steep, and the wheelbarrow felt like it weighed a ton. As we started to descend, I could feel the weight pulling me forward. I had to slow my steps to keep control.

Richard, of course, saw this as a challenge.

"Come on, Dullah, stop dragging your feet," he said with a smirk. Then, without warning, he picked up speed.

"Don’t!" I warned, but it was too late.

Richard was already racing ahead, pushing the wheelbarrow faster and faster down the hill. I gritted my teeth and tried to keep up, my hands gripping the handles tightly as the wheelbarrow began to wobble under the pressure. The sloshing sounds of the waste inside made me feel sick.

"Richard, slow down!" I shouted, but he just laughed and kept going.

I could hear Brian and Gerald standing at the top of the hill, shouting warnings and laughing as we tore down the slope. My heart was pounding, and all I could think about was how this was going to end badly.

And then it happened.

Richard’s wheelbarrow hit a rock, tipping sideways and spilling it's contents. I barely had time to react before mine followed suit. Both wheelbarrows overturned, sending a wave of foul-smelling liquid flying through the air. The next thing I knew, I was on the ground, covered in waste, my wheelbarrow on it's side.

But that wasn’t the worst part.

As I wiped the disgusting mess from my face, I saw it—*the new blue school minibus*. Parked at the bottom of the hill, and now covered in the sewage we’d just spilled. And standing next to it, looking horrified, was Mr. Miyagi.

I froze. Richard was on the ground next to me, looking equally stunned. The silence was deafening as the reality of what had just happened sank in. The school’s brand-new minibus—the one they’d only just gotten—was ruined. And Mr. Miyagi, our principal, was standing there, half-covered in sewage himself, his face a mask of shock.

"Oh no," I whispered, my voice barely audible.

"Oh yes," Mr. Miyagi said, his voice shaking with barely-contained fury.

Richard groaned, rolling over and staring up at the mess we’d made. "This... this is bad."

"Yeah," I said, wiping my face again. "Really bad."

Mr. Jones appeared a few moments later, his eyes wide as he took in the scene. He looked at me, then at Richard, then at the minibus, and finally at Mr. Miyagi, who was still standing in stunned silence.

"What... what happened here?" Mr. Jones asked, his voice low and dangerous.

Neither Richard nor I said a word. There wasn’t much we could say. The evidence was all around us.

Mr. Jones let out a long sigh, rubbing his temples as if trying to stave off a massive headache. "I don’t even know where to begin," he muttered.

I wanted to disappear. I wanted to be anywhere but here. Covered in waste, staring at the ruined school bus, I felt like this was rock bottom. And as much as I wanted to blame Richard, I knew we were both equally responsible for this disaster.

"You two," Mr. Jones finally said, his voice calm but firm. "Go clean yourselves up. We’ll deal with this later."

He didn’t have to tell us twice. Richard and I scrambled to our feet, still reeking of sewage, and hurried away from the scene, the laughter of the other students echoing behind us.

---


**Later that Evening**

As I trudged home, still smelling faintly of the day’s disaster despite scrubbing myself clean, all I could think about was how much trouble I was in. Not just with the school, but with Uncle Jan. There was no way this wouldn’t get back to him. And after today, I knew I’d have to face more than just Mr. Jones’ anger.

The worst part? I wasn’t even mad at Richard anymore. I was just exhausted. Exhausted from trying to keep up with him, exhausted from constantly getting into trouble, and exhausted from being the new kid who couldn’t seem to catch a break.

As I reached Uncle Jan’s farm, the goats bleating their usual greetings, I took a deep breath. Tomorrow was going to be worse—I could feel it. But for now, all I could do was collapse into bed and hope that somehow, someway, this whole mess would blow over.

But deep down, I knew it wouldn’t. This rivalry with Richard was far from over.

---


**End of Chapter 6**

---

## Chapter 7: Consequences and Reflection

---


**Tuesday, February 18th**

The next morning, walking to school felt like marching to my own funeral. The sun was out, the air was warm, but inside, I was cold, tense. My feet dragged along the dirt road, kicking up little clouds of dust as I went. All I could think about was the disaster that unfolded yesterday—the latrine spill, Mr. Miyagi standing there, half-covered in sewage, and the laughter of the other kids echoing around me.

This was it. There was no coming back from this. My rivalry with Richard had reached a boiling point, and the whole school knew about it. The fact that I had to face everyone again after what happened made my stomach twist. I dreaded every step that brought me closer to Low Water Primary.

As I walked through the school gates, I could already feel eyes on me. Whispers. Snickers. My shoulders tensed, and I tried to block it all out, heading straight for the classroom. I could already see Richard up ahead, standing with his usual group of friends. Brian was nearby, nervously fiddling with his shiny hair while Gerald and Mervin were talking about something I couldn’t quite catch.

But it wasn’t long before the laughter started.

---


**In the Classroom**

I walked into the classroom, and instantly, the whispers started swirling around me like flies. Kids giggled and nudged each other as I passed by. I could hear snippets of their conversations, but I tried to block it out.

"Did you see him yesterday?"
"How does anyone recover from that?"
"I’m surprised he even showed up."

I slumped down into my seat, trying to make myself as small as possible. Berenice was already at her desk, writing something in her notebook. When she saw me, she flashed a small smile, but I barely managed to return it.

She leaned over. "Don’t let them get to you, Abdullah. They’ll forget about it soon enough."

I appreciated the attempt, but I wasn’t so sure. The incident was too big, too gross, to just fade away like that.

Just as I was settling in, I noticed Richard enter the room. He had that smug look on his face that made my blood boil. He might have been covered in the same filth as me yesterday, but somehow, he always managed to come out looking like the victim. He strolled in like nothing had happened, as if the whole thing had been my fault.

And then, out of nowhere, the teasing took a turn.

"You and Richard look like such a cute couple, Dullah," one of the boys called out from the back of the room, setting off a ripple of laughter.

I clenched my fists under the desk, the anger rising. Richard’s eyes locked onto mine, and the smirk on his face only grew wider.

"Leave him alone, Gerald," Berenice’s voice rang out across the room, sharper than usual.

Suddenly, the laughter stopped.

She stood up, her chair scraping loudly against the floor. I hadn’t seen her this angry before. She marched right over to where Richard was standing with Gerald and the other boys who’d been teasing me.

"Richard, I’m sick of it," Berenice snapped. Her face was flushed, and she jabbed a finger at his chest. "I’m sick of you and your little group treating me like I’m your girlfriend. I am not your girlfriend, I never was your girlfriend—"

The whole classroom was dead silent now. Richard’s face paled, the smug look slipping away as Berenice tore into him.

"—and I am nobody’s girlfriend right now. Leave me alone to like who I like and spend time with who I choose!"

The finality in her words hit Richard like a slap across the face. His jaw clenched, and for a moment, it looked like he was going to say something. But instead, he just turned away, his fists tight by his sides.

The classroom erupted into whispers again, but this time, they weren’t about me. They were about Berenice’s outburst. She had just publicly shut Richard down in front of everyone, and I could tell by the look on his face that he wasn’t going to forget it anytime soon.

---


**Facing Uncle Jan**

That afternoon, the humiliation still hung heavy on my shoulders as I trudged home. The whole day had been a disaster. Despite Berenice’s defense, the teasing continued. The whispers and the laughter followed me everywhere, no matter how much I tried to ignore it.

But worse than that was the thought of what awaited me at home.

When I reached the farm, Uncle Jan was already waiting for me, standing by the goat pen with his arms crossed and a sour look on his face. My stomach sank. I knew the news of the latrine disaster had made it's way to him. There was no escaping the consequences now.

"You got anything to say for yourself?" he asked, his voice cold and sharp as a whip.

I swallowed hard. "It wasn’t... it wasn’t just me."

Uncle Jan’s eyes narrowed. "Oh, I know it wasn’t just you. But you’re the one standing in front of me right now, aren’t you?"

I couldn’t argue with that. I looked down at my feet, unable to meet his gaze.

"Do you have any idea what kind of trouble you’ve caused? What kind of embarrassment?" he continued, his voice steady but full of disappointment. "You’re supposed to represent this family here. And what have you done instead? You’ve made yourself a joke."

Each word cut deeper than the last. I’d rather he yelled at me, anything but this cold, quiet anger. I felt like a complete failure.

"I’ve already had a word with Mr. Jones," Uncle Jan added, crossing his arms tighter. "You’re lucky you didn’t get suspended. But from now on, you’ll be working extra hours on the farm, and you better get used to it. If you’ve got energy to cause trouble at school, you’ve got energy to do more work here."

There was nothing I could say. I nodded, knowing there was no room for negotiation. He turned away, and I knew the conversation was over.

---


**Reflection**

That evening, I stood in the goat pen, my hands raw from pulling weeds and feeding the stubborn animals. The sun was setting, casting long shadows over the farm, but the heaviness in my chest didn’t fade with the light.

I leaned against the fence, wiping the sweat from my brow, and stared out at the horizon. My mind kept replaying the last few days, trying to make sense of how things had spiraled out of control so quickly. The rivalry with Richard, the constant teasing, the humiliation—none of it seemed to end.

I thought about what Berenice had said earlier. The way she stood up to Richard, made it clear she wasn’t going to let him control her or decide who she could be friends with. For a moment, I admired her strength. But then I realized something—Berenice had stood up for herself. I hadn’t. I had let Richard’s taunts, his arrogance, get under my skin and push me into one mess after another.

And now, I was paying the price.

---


**Setting the Stage**

The next day at school, the tension was palpable. Richard wasn’t speaking to anyone. He avoided me at every turn, but I could feel his anger simmering just below the surface.

The teasing hadn’t stopped, but it had changed. People were now more interested in Berenice’s outburst than in the latrine disaster, which was both a relief and a new source of tension. Richard’s pride had taken a hit, and I knew it wasn’t over. He would find a way to make me pay for everything that had happened—especially for what Berenice had said.

By the time lunchtime rolled around, I felt the weight of the whole school watching us, waiting for something to happen. Berenice had been keeping her distance, and Brian—well, he was Brian, still making jokes, still trying to pretend like everything was fine. But it wasn’t.

And then, as if the universe was setting us up for another disaster, Mr. Jones made an announcement at the end of the day.

"There will be an important assembly at the end of the week," he said, his voice carrying over the chatter of the students. "I expect all of you to be on your best behavior."

Assembly. That meant everyone in one place. And somehow, I just knew it was going to be another disaster waiting to happen. The tension between me and Richard had reached it's boiling point.

Something was going to give.

---


**End of Chapter 7**

## Chapter 8: The Final Conflict

**Friday, February 21st**

The air was thick with anticipation. Every student in the school was lined up in neat rows on the dusty patch of earth in front of the main building. The sun was high, and I could feel it's heat pressing down on us like a weight. It matched the heaviness in my chest as we stood for the weekly assembly.

Mr. Jones was at the front, pacing slowly as he gave his usual speech about discipline and "making better choices." But his words barely registered with me. I could feel my heart pounding in my ears. Everything that had happened over the past few weeks—the teasing, the rivalry with Richard, the latrine disaster, Berenice snapping at Richard—it all seemed to be leading to this moment.

I glanced over at Richard, who was standing a few rows away. His face was unreadable, but his fists were clenched at his sides. Ever since Berenice had shut him down in front of everyone, he’d been keeping his distance. But I could feel the anger radiating off him, simmering just beneath the surface. And today, something felt different. The tension between us was like a live wire, buzzing and ready to snap.

"…and that’s why it’s important," Mr. Jones’ voice rang out, "that each of you takes responsibility for your actions."

His eyes swept over the crowd, pausing for a moment on me and Richard. It was clear the message was meant for us, though he didn’t say it outright.

Suddenly, a loud whistle cut through the silence, drawing everyone’s attention. I turned to see Morgan, one of the boys from our class, nudging Brian and pointing at Dora, who was standing just a few rows ahead of us. She was barefoot, her long, sharp toenails digging into the dirt like talons. It was the same joke they’d been making since Grade 3\.

Morgan started whistling again, louder this time, and Richard smirked, egging him on.

"Careful, Brian," Morgan said, just loud enough for a few others to hear. "She might scratch you next!"

The boys nearby burst into laughter. I glanced at Dora. Her face flushed red with anger and embarrassment, but she didn’t say anything. She just glared at Morgan, fists clenched at her sides.

The laughter grew louder, and soon, other students were joining in. Mr. Jones, standing at the front, was too busy talking to notice what was happening. But I saw it. I saw the moment when Dora had enough.

With a quick, angry movement, she swung her foot out and scratched Morgan’s calf with her long toenails. He yelped in pain, stumbling backward as blood trickled down his leg.

The laughter stopped. Everything froze for a second as the entire assembly fell silent. Mr. Jones spun around, eyes narrowed, as he tried to figure out what had just happened.

"WHAT is going on here?" Mr. Jones’ voice thundered through the silence.

Morgan clutched his leg, still grimacing, and pointed accusingly at Dora. "She scratched me!"

Mr. Jones’ eyes scanned the crowd, and in an instant, his gaze landed on me. It didn’t matter that I hadn’t done anything. It never did.

"Abdullah!" he snapped, his voice sharp. "And Richard! Both of you—outside the office. Now!"

I blinked in shock. "But I didn’t—"

"NOW!" Mr. Jones cut me off, his tone leaving no room for argument.

I could feel the eyes of the entire school on me as I stepped out of line, my heart sinking. Richard followed behind me, his face set in a hard, defiant expression. This wasn’t just about Dora and Morgan. Mr. Jones was making an example out of us.

---


**Outside Mr. Jones’ Office**

The bench outside Mr. Jones’ office had never felt more uncomfortable. I sat there, my hands trembling slightly as I rested them in my lap, waiting for the inevitable punishment. Richard sat beside me, arms crossed, staring straight ahead with a scowl on his face.

The other boys—Morgan, Francois, Gerald—had already been called into the office. I could hear the sharp crack of the cane through the door, followed by muffled whimpers of pain. Each time the door opened, another boy came out, face red and eyes watery, and then disappeared down the hall. I knew it was only a matter of time before it was my turn.

The door opened again, and Francois emerged, rubbing his backside with a grimace. Mr. Jones’ voice followed him out. "Next!"

My stomach dropped. This was it. I braced myself, pushing off the bench to stand. But before I could move, I heard Richard mutter something under his breath.

"You shouldn’t even be here," he said, his voice low and full of resentment.

I froze. "What did you just say?"

Richard finally turned to look at me, his eyes cold. "You don’t belong here. You should’ve stayed in Congo."

The words hit me like a punch to the gut. My heart pounded, and suddenly, everything I had been holding in—the anger, the frustration, the loneliness—boiled over.

I took a step toward him, fists clenched at my sides. "What did you say?" I asked again, my voice shaking with barely contained fury.

"You heard me," Richard said, standing up to face me. "You think you’re so great because you can run fast? Because Berenice likes you? You don’t belong here. You’ll never belong here."

For a moment, everything blurred. I could feel the anger coursing through me, begging me to lash out. All the humiliation, all the teasing, the taunts, the rivalry—it all came rushing to the surface. My fists tightened, and I could feel the heat rising in my chest.

I was done.

I took another step closer, my body trembling with the urge to hit him. To show him that I wasn’t the weak, scared new kid he thought I was.

But then something stopped me.

A voice—my mother’s voice—echoed in my mind. The stories she used to tell me when I was little. About how, no matter what happened, no matter how much people tried to bring us down, we had to rise above it. To be better.

I froze, fists still clenched, staring at Richard. His face twisted into a sneer, like he was daring me to hit him, to take the bait.

But I didn’t. I couldn’t.

Because hitting him wouldn’t make me feel better. It wouldn’t fix anything. It wouldn’t change the fact that I missed my parents. That I was far from home. That I was still trying to find my place in this new world.

It wouldn’t change who I was.

So I did the hardest thing I could think of.

I stepped back.

Richard’s sneer faltered. "What? Too scared?"

I shook my head, my fists slowly unclenching. "No. I’m not scared," I said, my voice steady now. "I just don’t need to prove anything to you."

The door to Mr. Jones’ office swung open, and he stepped out, cane in hand, glaring at the two of us. "Abdullah, Richard. Inside. Now."

I took a deep breath, my heart still racing, but I felt lighter somehow. Like a weight had been lifted. I had made my choice.

As we stepped into the office, I knew there would be consequences. I would face the punishment, just like the others. But this time, it was different. This time, I wasn’t running from who I was.

And for the first time since I arrived in South Africa, I felt like I was finally standing on solid ground.

---


**End of Chapter 8**

## Chapter 9: Abdullah Snaps and Runs

---


Abdullah’s fists clenched at his sides as he stood over Richard, every muscle in his body tense. Richard was on the ground, smirking despite everything, egging him on with a look that seemed to say, *Go ahead, hit me.* The words Richard had spat out—telling Abdullah he didn’t belong—echoed in his mind, fueling his anger. His knuckles tightened, and for a second, he thought about it. About giving in, letting his fist connect with Richard’s face. Maybe then it would end. Maybe then Richard would understand.

But just as quickly, he stopped himself. He wasn’t going to give Richard the satisfaction. Not like this. Not here.

His breathing slowed, and he took a step back, loosening his fists. He wouldn’t do it.

Before he could make sense of the emotions swirling inside him, the door to Mr. Jones’ office swung open. Mr. Jones stepped out, his eyes hard as they locked onto Abdullah. "Abdullah!" he barked, voice slicing through the tension. "If you force me to come get you, you’ll regret it."

Abdullah’s chest tightened. He knew that tone, that threat. He had heard it too many times before. He could feel the weight of Mr. Jones’ authority pressing down on him, trapping him. And in that moment, something snapped.

He wasn’t going to get hit for something he didn’t even do. Not again.

The walls of the school office felt like they were closing in around him as Mr. Jones grabbed his shoulder, steering him toward the door. The other boys stood by, watching, waiting to see what would happen next. Richard climbed to his feet, still sneering, and the smirk on his face was the last straw.

Abdullah yanked his arm free from Mr. Jones’ grip and bolted.

"Abdullah!" Mr. Jones’ voice roared behind him, but Abdullah didn’t stop. His feet pounded against the dirt as he raced toward the school gate, every instinct in his body screaming at him to run. He didn’t know where he was going—he just needed to get away.

Behind him, the sound of Mr. Jones yelling orders faded as he gained distance. He sprinted down the dirt path that led away from the school, heart pounding in his chest. He could hear the shouts of the boys on the porch, their voices carried by the wind. The last thing he caught was Mr. Jones shouting, "Get the bakkie!"

---


**The Chase Begins**

Abdullah ran harder, faster than he ever had before. The dry, dusty road stretched out ahead of him, and he focused on the familiar landscape, trying to keep his breathing steady. His mind was racing just as fast as his legs. He couldn’t go back—not after this. He needed to escape, to get away from the punishments, the rivalry, the pressure. For a fleeting moment, he imagined running all the way back to Congo, back to the life he knew before everything fell apart.

The sound of an engine roared in the distance, and Abdullah’s heart jumped in his chest. He glanced over his shoulder and saw Mr. Jones in the bakkie, the school’s pickup truck, barreling down the hill toward him. In the back of the truck, he could see Gerald, Morgan, Brian, and Richard, leaning over the edge, calling out and catcalling like they were watching a game.

Abdullah’s legs burned as he pushed himself faster, but the bakkie was closing in. He needed to get off the road, to find somewhere to hide. Up ahead, he spotted the narrow one-car bridge that crossed the river—a wooden bridge usually occupied by a herd of cows at this time of day. If he could just get across, the bakkie would have to stop.

---


**The Bridge Full of Cows**

The bridge came into view, and just as he’d hoped, it was packed with cows, their large bodies blocking the way. Abdullah darted toward the bridge, weaving through the cows, slipping between their slow, lumbering movements. He could hear the bakkie screech to a halt behind him as Mr. Jones slammed on the brakes.

"Move the cows!" Gerald shouted from the back of the truck, his voice filled with excitement.

"Come on, you stupid animals!" Morgan whistled and waved his arms, trying to herd the cows off the bridge. The boys in the back of the bakkie laughed, enjoying the chaos.

But while the others were focused on the cows, one of them wasn’t. Richard.

Richard didn’t wait. He leapt off the back of the bakkie and hit the ground running, his eyes locked on Abdullah. There was no hesitation in his movements, no mocking laughter. This wasn’t a game to him. He was chasing Abdullah for real, and Abdullah could feel him gaining ground.

---


**The Chase Tightens**

Abdullah’s lungs burned, and his legs felt like lead as he pushed himself harder. He was fast—he knew that—but Richard had the stamina for long distances. It was only a matter of time before he caught up. Every second, every step brought Richard closer.

"Come on!" Abdullah muttered to himself, glancing at the trees and bushes lining the road, searching for an escape. He needed to hide, to disappear. Vonnie’s spaza shop wasn’t far now. If he could just reach it, he could slip behind the shop and find somewhere to think, to plan his next move.

Twenty steps. Just twenty steps to freedom.

But then he heard the scream.

---


**Richard in Danger**

Abdullah’s heart skipped a beat as the scream pierced the air. He spun around, skidding to a stop. Richard was surrounded by three dogs—stray, vicious-looking animals, their teeth bared, growling and snapping at him. His shirt was off, and he was swinging it wildly, trying to fend them off, but it wasn’t working. The dogs were closing in, teeth flashing in the sun.

Fear froze Abdullah in place for a second. He could hear Richard yelling, panicking, but the dogs weren’t backing off. In that instant, everything between them—the rivalry, the anger, the taunts—faded away. Richard wasn’t his enemy right now. He was just a kid, terrified and cornered.

Without thinking, Abdullah grabbed a half-broken brick from the side of the road and flung it at one of the dogs. The brick hit the dog’s side with a dull thud, and the animal yelped, backing off for a moment. Abdullah didn’t stop. He rushed forward, kicking and shouting, swinging his arms at the other two dogs.

The dogs hesitated, unsure of the new threat, and Abdullah used the moment to push Richard toward the edge of the road. They stood back to back, panting, both boys terrified but determined. The dogs circled them, growling, but now that they were together, they stood their ground.

"Stay close," Abdullah muttered, his voice low.

Richard nodded, too out of breath to respond. His eyes were wide with fear, his shirt still clutched in one hand as a makeshift weapon. But together, they fought off the dogs, yelling and kicking until the animals finally retreated, their snarls fading into the distance.

---


**Brothers Instead of Rivals**

For a long moment, the two boys just stood there, breathing hard, shoulders touching, the adrenaline still pumping through their veins. They were bruised, dirty, but they had made it. Together.

Richard, still catching his breath, looked at Abdullah with something different in his eyes. There was no smirk, no arrogance. Just a quiet, unspoken respect.

He gave a small nod, almost imperceptible. "Thanks," he said, his voice hoarse.

Abdullah nodded back, feeling the weight of everything they’d been through lift slightly. He didn’t say anything. He didn’t need to. They both knew things had changed.

As they started walking back toward the school, the rivalry that had once burned so hot between them felt... distant. They weren’t enemies anymore. Maybe not friends yet, but something more like brothers. Brothers who had faced danger side by side.

And for the first time in weeks, Abdullah felt like he wasn’t running away.

---


**End of Chapter 9**

## Chapter 10: A Fight for Survival, Not Rivalry

---


Abdullah and Richard stood still for a moment, their bodies tense, chests heaving with exhaustion after driving the dogs away. The dust settled around them, and the snarls of the dogs faded into the distance, but their hearts still pounded from the chaos of the last few minutes.

Abdullah could hardly believe it. Just moments ago, he had been running from Richard and everything that represented his new life. Now, they were standing back to back, having just fought off three vicious dogs together. The rivalry that had burned so hot between them felt distant, replaced by something neither of them could quite define. They were no longer enemies.

Richard was the first to move, wiping the sweat off his forehead and shaking his head in disbelief. That was insane, he muttered, his voice still hoarse from the chase and the fight.

Abdullah, still catching his breath, nodded. His legs ached from running, and his muscles throbbed from the adrenaline. Yeah, was all he could manage to say.

For a moment, they stood in silence, each processing what had just happened. The tension between them, the chase, the dogs—it was all swirling in their minds, but something had changed. The edge that used to be between them had softened.

Richard turned toward Abdullah, eyes no longer filled with competition but with something closer to respect. He gave a quick nod, a silent acknowledgment of what they’d just been through together. Thanks… for coming back, Richard said, still sounding unsure of himself.

Abdullah shrugged. You would’ve done the same, he replied, though neither of them was entirely sure if that was true.

---


**The Journey Back**

The adrenaline was fading now, and with it came a dull ache in Abdullah’s legs. His shirt clung to his back, soaked with sweat, and the sun felt hotter than ever as it beat down on the dirt road. Without a word, the two boys began walking back toward the school. They moved slowly at first, each step heavy with exhaustion, but the silence between them wasn’t uncomfortable—it was a shared understanding that something had shifted.

As they walked, Abdullah’s mind wandered back to what had happened just before the dogs attacked. The chase had been about proving something—Richard trying to show that he was better, faster, stronger. And Abdullah had been running not just from Richard, but from the frustration, the anger, the feeling of always being on the outside.

But now? Now things were different.

After a few minutes of walking, Richard broke the silence. You’re fast, he said, almost begrudgingly. But you burn out quick.

Abdullah let out a small laugh. And you can’t sprint if your life depended on it.

Richard gave a tired grin. I guess I’ve got more stamina. His voice held no malice now, just an observation. For the first time, it wasn’t a competition—it was just a fact.

They continued walking, the tension between them gone. Abdullah glanced over at Richard and caught a glimpse of the boy who had been his rival for so long, but now he just saw someone who had been as scared as he was. And for the first time since he arrived in South Africa, he didn’t feel like he was alone.

As they approached the school, the bakkie came into view. The cows had cleared off the bridge, and Mr. Jones stood with his hands on his hips, glaring in their direction. The other boys were still hanging around the bakkie, but their laughter had died down. They were watching now—watching as Abdullah and Richard walked back together.

---


**Facing Mr. Jones**

Abdullah and Richard both stopped a few meters away from Mr. Jones, the weight of what they had done settling back into their minds. There was no doubt in their minds that they were in for it. The entire school had seen Abdullah run, and now they were returning after who knew how long, bruised, dirty, and clearly having been in trouble.

Mr. Jones didn’t say anything at first. He just looked at them—really looked—and seemed to see that something was different. His mouth was set in a thin line, but his eyes flickered between Abdullah and Richard, as if trying to figure out what had just happened between them.

Inside. Now, he finally said, his voice low but firm.

Abdullah’s stomach dropped, and for a moment, he thought about running again. But instead, he gave a quick nod and followed Richard inside, feeling the weight of the other boys’ eyes on his back.

As they walked through the doors of the school, Mr. Jones followed close behind, his heavy footsteps echoing through the quiet hallways. The rest of the school must have been watching from the classroom windows, waiting to see what punishment awaited them.

Mr. Jones ushered them into his office, where the familiar wooden desk stood like a barrier between them and the impending consequences. Sit, he ordered.

Abdullah sank into the chair, his mind racing. He couldn’t shake the feeling that everything was about to fall apart again, but there was something different this time. He wasn’t alone. Richard sat next to him, quiet and composed, no longer the smug boy from earlier.

---


**The Unexpected Turn**

Mr. Jones leaned back in his chair, eyes scanning both boys with a look that made it clear he was trying to make sense of the situation. He hadn’t expected them to come back together, not like this.

You two, Mr. Jones began, shaking his head slightly. I’ve been dealing with this nonsense between you for weeks. Running off like that… fighting dogs in the street… What’s next? What do I have to do to get through to you?

Richard and Abdullah exchanged a glance, both knowing that they had crossed a line today. But before either of them could respond, Mr. Jones continued.

You both could’ve gotten seriously hurt today. And for what? To prove something? To settle some ridiculous score?

The boys were silent. There was no point in arguing.

Mr. Jones sighed, rubbing his temples. I’m not going to punish you the way I should. Not today. You’ve clearly been through enough. He paused, looking at them closely. But I expect things to change between you two. This… whatever this rivalry has been, it ends now. Understood?

Richard nodded immediately, his expression serious. Yes, sir.

Abdullah followed suit, a weight lifting off his shoulders. Yes, sir.

Mr. Jones eyed them both for another long moment before finally sitting back in his chair. Go home. And don’t let me see you in here again.

---


**A New Beginning**

The walk home was quiet but not uncomfortable. The rivalry between Abdullah and Richard felt like a distant memory now, replaced by something else—something more like mutual respect. They weren’t suddenly best friends, but there was an unspoken understanding between them. They had been through something together, and it had changed everything.

As they parted ways at the school gate, Richard gave Abdullah a small wave, the tension between them completely gone. See you tomorrow, Dullah.

Yeah, see you, Abdullah replied, feeling lighter than he had in weeks.

As he walked home, his mind wandered back to what Mr. Jones had said. The rivalry was over, but that didn’t mean the challenges were. He still had to figure out who he was in this new world, still had to find his place in South Africa. But now, for the first time, he felt like he could face it—whatever it was.

He was no longer running away. He was standing his ground.

---


**End of Chapter 10**

## Chapter 11: Resolution and New Beginnings

---


The next morning, the air felt lighter.

Abdullah walked the familiar path to school, the dust rising under his feet as the sun slowly climbed into the sky. For the first time since arriving in South Africa, the knot in his stomach had loosened. The tension that had plagued him for weeks—the rivalry, the constant feeling of being an outsider—was gone, or at least, it had shifted into something new, something manageable.

When he reached the school gate, he spotted Richard leaning against the wall, casually waiting for him. Abdullah raised an eyebrow as he approached, unsure of what to expect. There was no tension in Richard’s stance, no arrogance in his eyes—just an easy nod of acknowledgment.

Morning, Richard said, his voice neutral but with a hint of something softer than before. It wasn’t an apology, but it was close enough.

Morning, Abdullah replied, offering a small smile.

They walked into the schoolyard together, not as best friends, but as something more than rivals. The other students watched them, murmurs buzzing through the crowd as they noticed the change. It was clear something had happened, and the way the two boys walked side by side said more than any words could.

---


**Mr. Jones’ Classroom**

When they stepped into the classroom, the usual chatter died down. The students exchanged glances, some surprised, some just curious. Berenice gave Abdullah a quick nod, her eyes twinkling with approval. Brian, as usual, couldn’t help himself. He sauntered up to the two boys with an exaggerated grin.

Well, well, well, Brian said, rubbing his hands together. Looks like the gladiators have laid down their swords.

Abdullah rolled his eyes, but he couldn’t help smiling. Something like that.

Richard just shook his head, though there was a trace of a grin on his face too. Don’t push it, Brian.

Before Brian could respond, the classroom door swung open, and Mr. Jones entered, carrying his usual stack of papers. His eyes scanned the room, briefly resting on Abdullah and Richard. For a moment, the corner of his mouth twitched, almost like he was trying not to smile, but he quickly masked it with his usual stern expression.

Alright, settle down, Mr. Jones said, clapping his hands. Let’s get to work.

The lesson went by quickly, the tension that had once filled the classroom now a distant memory. Abdullah found himself more relaxed, more focused, even when Mr. Jones called on him to answer questions. There was no longer the pressure to prove himself, no need to compete with Richard for attention or approval.

It felt like a fresh start.

---


**Lunchtime and Soccer Rematch**

At lunch, the usual crowd gathered on the field for soccer. Abdullah and Richard both laced up their shoes, and the teams naturally formed, though now with a more balanced energy between them. The playful rivalry between them was still there, but now it felt fun, like they were pushing each other to get better rather than trying to tear each other down.

The game was fast-paced, filled with shouts of encouragement and friendly jabs. Richard and Abdullah ended up on opposite teams, but every time they faced off, there was a smile on their faces, not a scowl. When Abdullah scored the final goal, sealing the win for his team, Richard laughed, shaking his head.

Alright, I’ll give you that one, Richard said, walking over and clapping Abdullah on the back.

Abdullah grinned. You’ll get me next time.

It was a promise, not a challenge. A sign of things to come—friendly competition instead of bitter rivalry.

As they headed back to the school building, Berenice caught up with Abdullah, her usual bright smile on her face. You’re different today, she said, falling into step beside him.

I guess things are different now, Abdullah replied, glancing back at Richard, who was joking around with the other boys.

Berenice gave him a knowing look. It suits you.

---


**Facing Uncle Jan**

Later that afternoon, Abdullah walked home from school with a sense of peace he hadn’t felt in a long time. The sun was low in the sky, casting long shadows across the dirt road as he made his way back to Uncle Jan’s farm.

When he reached the gate, he saw Uncle Jan working by the goat pen, as usual. The older man glanced up as Abdullah approached, his eyes sharp and assessing. Abdullah hadn’t told him much about what had happened at school, but he was sure the news would have made it's way back to the farm.

Uncle Jan straightened up, wiping his hands on his worn work pants. Heard you didn’t run into trouble today, he said, his voice gruff but not unkind.

Abdullah shrugged, trying to play it off casually. Not today.

Uncle Jan gave a short nod, his gaze lingering on Abdullah for a moment longer than usual. Then, without another word, he turned back to his work, but not before giving Abdullah a small, rare smile—a gesture of approval that carried more weight than any words could.

Abdullah smiled to himself as he walked toward the house, feeling like he had taken a big step forward, not just with Richard but with Uncle Jan too.

---


**A New Challenge Looms**

That evening, after dinner, Abdullah sat at his small desk, going through his homework. The room was quiet, save for the distant sounds of the farm—the goats bleating softly, the rustling of wind through the trees. His mind wandered back to the events of the past few days. So much had changed in such a short time, and yet it all felt right.

But just as he started to relax, a knock came at his door.

Uncle Jan stood in the doorway, holding a plain white envelope in his hand. His expression was unreadable as he passed it to Abdullah. This came for you.

Abdullah’s heart skipped a beat as he took the envelope. The handwriting was unfamiliar, and there was no return address. His fingers trembled slightly as he tore it open.

The letter inside was short, the words scrawled in hurried handwriting.

*Abdullah, there are things you need to know about your parents. About why they fought. Be ready.*

There was no signature. Just those few cryptic sentences.

Abdullah stared at the letter, his mind racing. What could this mean? Why now?

He folded the letter carefully, setting it on his desk. The peace he had felt earlier in the day was now overshadowed by a growing sense of unease. The rivalry with Richard might have come to an end, but it seemed that his journey was far from over.

Whatever this was, it was only the beginning.
